messages.body_plain:
Dear prospective students for R / GSoC 2010,

Something we discussed among the mentors (and which you may have heard from
the mentor you are working with) is that you really should submit your
proposals sooner rather than later.

Remember that the proposals get voted upon by all mentors, so you want many
eyeballs on your proposal early rather than late.

And once submitted, you can still edit, enhance, augment, clarify, ... at
will.  Following the 'many eyeballs make all bugs shallow' principle in open
source, you are likely to be better off by submitting early and having many
proof readers rather than discussing with just your mentor.

So please plan on submitting within the next day or two -- as opposed to at
the very end of the deadline near April 9.

Feel free to send questions back to the list here.

Regards,  Dirk

messages.subject: Project Idea: Web-Based Graphing
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm very interested in participating in GSOC 2010, and wanted to pass an idea by those subscribing to this list. I've been exploring different ways of making interactive graphs and data visualizations for the web. I'm a huge fan of R, and one of my wishes for the software package is to be able to easily create and export interactive graphs to the web.

While this project is not as statistically intense as some of the current proposals, I believe it's a perfect GSOC project. This is mainly because I think the entire project could be started and completed within the GSOC time frame. Furthermore, judging by the large amount of interest in data visualization, such a project could be a huge benefit for R.

For the sake of brevity, I don't want to go into the technical details of the proposal. The deliverable of such a project would be an R package that would allow users to export interactive graphs and data visualizations to a web-friendly format. At the very least, it would provide a large number of the basic graphing functions that R already provides, and the visualizations would be easily customizable.

Is there anyone who would be interested in mentoring this? Does anyone think it would be of use to R users?

Thank you,
Wojciech

messages.subject_clean: Project idea: use of R on web-pages
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
for a long time I have an idea and, I think, GSOC is a good
possibility to implement this.

Two main parts of web applications are user part (web-page) and
storage of data (DB). Often statistical work has to be done on data
and presented to a user. Simple example: average temperature at a day
on a meteorological site. Complicated example: some statistics and
graphics concerning financial time series. Usually, special business
logic is created to implement these statistical functions.

I propose to implement this in R. Separate R-functions will get data
from DB and return necessary information to the user-part. Names of
the functions will be parameters to JSTL-tags.

Advantages:
1) we can use all the huge number of R-functions without implementing
them.
2) It allows change R-code without changing other parts and even
without recompiling the application.

I know, there is a possibility to call R from Java. Interactive
graphics can be implemented in Flex.

This is the main idea. Technical details should be specified.

Has this idea future? Has anybody interest in mentoring this?
Waiting for your response.

ConstantinM

Hi Wojciech,

Your initial proposal looks promising, but I'd like to see more
details about the interface. Would you be able to export a plot
created by R's currently graphics systems (base and grid)? Or would
you provide your own set of high-level functions?  If so, what would
they be? Or would you only provide low-level functions that the user
would use to assemble their own plots? If so, what? What types of
interaction would you facilitate that aren't currently possible within
R?

In fact, I suspect much of what you have pencilled in the initial
research phase needs to be done now, so that we have some way of
assessing the likelihood of success of your project.  This is probably
a good idea because as it is I think your timetable is far too
ambitious - in my opinion it's just not possible to create a powerful,
flexible and extensible graphics package in a single month.

Hadley

messages.subject_clean: Proposal- Javascript client for R using nixysa framework
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

   The web is becoming more and more dominant platform. That's why I
want to expose the idea of the cross-browser client for R using nixysa
project.

   Nixysa is a framework that lets you write code in c++, then
generates NPAPI(Netscape Plug-in Application Programming Interface)
compatible code and, using scons, builds a plug-in on any platform, so
that you can use its functionality from JavaScript. Nixysa works with
most of the platforms and browsers.

The project idea is to create:
   - custom R graphics driver targetting the HTML5 canvas tag,
forwarding low level drawing instructions to the dynamic page in real
time, so that we can use R graphics in the browser.
   - static plug-in(R embedded into the plug-in) that takes R
instructions from JavaScript code and, using nixysa, returns the
result/code directly into the html/js document.(Rcpp and Rinside
frameworks)
   - client for R running remotely.(using Rserve)

Advantages:
 - full interactivity with R
 - cross-platform and cross-browser support
 - native HTML/JavaScript code (there is no need to install any other
plug-in)

Disadvantages:
 - security

If you have any questions please don't hesitate to ask me.

Konstantin Gorodinskiy

Hi everyone,

Thanks so much for all the feedback. Below are some detailed responses (under headings, to make life easier)...

Functions and Interface

When I initially started considering this project, I was thinking of creating actual functions that would make interactive, web-friendly plots. For example, one can easily use plot(x, y) to get a scatterplot or line plot. The Summer of Code package would instead have a new function, gsoc.plot(x, y, "/graph.html") which would save the scatterplot in a web-friendly format, and as a default, provide features like mouseover effects for different points.

To enable something like this, there would be underlying functions that one would use to draw the plots, in much the same way that one can use text(), lines(), etc. to add to plots in R. I'd also create new lower-level functions for making things interactive. Rather than having text(), I can also have mouseover.text() for mouseover text effects, for example.

Just to be clear, this project would focus on allowing R to export interactive graphics to the web.

Meta-Frameworks, Modifying Packages, etc.

I like the idea of a meta-framework, but I also think that within the Summer of Code time frame, this might be difficult.

In terms of modifying existing packages to make them web-friendly, I've thought about this as well. Technically, existing packages that allow one to save a plot as a JPG file or PDF are already "web-friendly" in that one can post those on the web and any browser will display them... The difficulty lies in making them interactive and really leveraging JavaScript, Flash, etc. to take advantage of features that static images lack.

With this in mind, I'd prefer to make my own package rather than modify existing ones or make wrappers for static images. I could easily make a wrapper so that would export a static plot into a JavaScript file that draws SVG images in a web browser, but this would still lack the interactivity that makes graphs so useful on the web.

I generally like to be flexible with my coding, and I would write the package in a way that would facilitate switching between different frameworks or libraries. For example, making it as easy as possible to have the package export graphics into JavaScript libraries like Raphael or into something like Adobe Flex. I'd shy away from calling this a meta-framework or anything like that, though, but it could be the seeds of one.

In my opinion, the big challenge is making a package that provides interactivity with enough customizability that people can make plots and graphs that do not follow a strict format. For example, it would be easy to have users make scatter plots where mousing over a point shows the (x, y) coordinates for that point. One can easily make it so colours are customized. However, it would be a bit more difficult to provide underlying functions that allow the user to decide how mouseover effects work (i.e. fade in? show up in a status bar rather than above the cursor? etc...).

I'm confident I could make a package that is both flexible and provides useful plotting features, though.

As far as I understand, Processing is great (I like it a lot!) but requires you to have a Java applet if you want to display graphics in a web page. If I'm wrong, I would be delighted to know it! In general, I'd like to avoid applets as they take a long time to load and aren't very pretty. Any thoughts?

Sincerely,

messages.body_plain:
- The goal of my project is to create an easy way to access R
functionality from web browser.

I want user to be able to write instructions like:
R rObj;//initialize the R-plugin in .js or .html file
rObj.eval(“x <- seq(0, 7, length=100)”);
rObj.eval(“y <- dlnorm(x)”);
rObj.eval(“plot(x,y,xlab="x",ylab="DLog(x)")”);

in js or html document, and to be able to get the plot within browser
with native HTML5/js code, without having to install any other plug-
ins or using applets.

- There is SNetscape package(http://www.omegahat.org/SNetscape/)
The problem there is that it uses Java applets to draw graphics. Today
with help of new HTML5 features such as canvas we can do complex
things in the browser without having to install additional packages.

Here is the example of drawing plot (sinus function) I wrote. It's
using HTML5 canvas tag:
http://gorodinskiy.org/plotExample/

- Suggested timeline is:
1. Implementing plug-in architecture that will accept R
instructions(in R syntax) and give
back result/code (1 week)
2. Wrapping R functionality into the plug-in (2-3 weeks)
3. Writing js layer to draw different graphics information and testing
them across all
browsers that support HTML 5 (1-2 week).
4. Modifying plug-in so to give back code to draw graphics to js/html
document(3 days)
5. Testing using different R instructions(2 weeks minimum)

Konstantin Gorodinskiy

messages.subject_clean: R and the Google Summer of Code 2010 -- Please welcome our new students!
messages.body_plain:
Earlier today Google finalised student / mentor pairings and allocations for
the Google Summer of Code 2010 (GSoC 2010).  The R Project is happy to
announce that the following students have been accepted:

   Colin Rundel, "rgeos - an R wrapper for GEOS", mentored by Roger Bivand of
      the Norges Handelshoyskole, Norway

   Ian Fellows, "A GUI for Graphics using ggplot2 and Deducer", mentored by
      Hadley Wickham of Rice University, USA

   Chidambaram Annamalai, "rdx - Automatic Differentiation in R", mentored by
      John Nash of University of Ottawa, Canada

   Yasuhisa Yoshida, "NoSQL interface for R", mentored by Dirk Eddelbuettel,
      Chicago, USA

   Felix Schoenbrodt, "Social Relations Analyses in R", mentored by Stefan
      Schmukle, Universitaet Muenster, Germany

   Details about all proposals are on the R Wiki page for the GSoC 2010 at
   http://rwiki.sciviews.org/doku.php?id=developers:projects:gsoc2010

The R Project is honoured to have received its highest number of student
allocations yet, and looks forward to an exciting Summer of Code.  Please
join me in welcoming our new students.

At this time, I would also like to thank all the other students who have
applied for working with R in this Summer of Code. With a limited number of
available slots, not all proposals can be accepted -- but I hope that those
not lucky enough to have been granted a slot will continue to work with R and
towards making contributions within the R world.

I would also like to express my thanks to all other mentors who provided for
a record number of proposals.  Without mentors and their project ideas we
would not have a Summer of Code -- so hopefully we will see you again next
year.

   Regards,

   Dirk (acting as R/GSoC 2010 admin)

--
  Regards, Dirk

--

messages.subject: Next (baby) steps: Common blog?
messages.body_plain:
Having worked with the two previous GSoC iterations, I had a chance to go the
end-of-summer wrap up sessions at Google. That was a good opportunity to
learn from other organisations about what works, what helps, ...

And one lesson seems to be to keep communication flowing.  Some organisations
even enforce weekly reports between students and mentors.  I was hoping that
we could do something a little less formal.  How would folks feel about, say,
a joint wiki page or maybe a joint blog?

So maybe one of the students could register a new blog at one of the free
services like blogger, wordpress, ... and then (off-list) share the
credentials with the other four.  That way we would end up with one place to
go for status updates and flow of information. It may even allow for
'comments'.

But that is just me thinking out aloud.  We could also use the R Wiki, or
mail summaries.  Thoughts? Comments?

These next few weeks are meant to sort some of these things out.  If there
are other questions or suggestions please do not hesitate and bring'em on!

--
  Regards, Dirk
